speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, many schools across the globe had to close during lockdowns and for prolonged periods and many schools are still closed in some countries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In Singapore, the entire teaching and education sector including from pre-school, Primary, Secondary, SPED, Junior Colleges, Polytechnics, ITE, private and international schools and our Universities, including CET centres and training providers and adult educators, including the entire MOE had to pivot and moved to home-based and online learning overnight.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many had to grapple with these new ways of work and education delivery.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many had to learn to use various video conferencing software.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Everyone had to convert their homes to become lecture theatres, virtual classrooms and even laboratories.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Notwithstanding, the entire education eco-system came together to pivot and to get our students get back to school after the circuit breaker and resume some normalcy including restarting many of the CCAs and events.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We thank every one of them who have made possible the delivery of education, skills and training to our students and adult learners against all odds, safely, in a social distance way.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With disruption, and now the dreaded disease, it is vital for the entire education system to stay ready, relevant and resilient.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I wish to highlight some pertinent points and observations for MOE for its entire education and learning continuum.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, seamless transition from Kindergarten 2 to Primary 1.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As MOE is now involved in delivering pre-school education through the MOE Kindergartens, I see an immense possibility and scope for MOE to better research into and enhance the curriculum of kindergartens as well as for Primary 1, so that we can better integrate and support the seamless transition of children from Kindergarten 2 to Primary 1.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I find that this is an important aspect which can be further augmented to ensure children are able to catch up with or sometimes cope with the knowledge, skills and competency requirements for Primary 1.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Two, strengthen mental health and wellness in schools.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We work for home and home-based learning as well as the bane that comes along with social media and device usage, as well as bullying both in the real and online world, the mental state, health, and well-being of students and teachers as well, from Primary all the way to University, is something we cannot take lightly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that our education system must be well poised and prepared to prevent, detect, and provide support this area in the next normal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Three, better prospects for Mother Tongue and Specialist Teachers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our Mother Tongue and other Specialist educators and teachers in school play an integral part and role in our education system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am particularly concerned especially in the treatment of and the parity of teachers who specifically teach only Art, Physical Education and Music and other specialised areas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Another area I feel strongly is the provision of job opportunities for SPED students and their future beyond the learning institutions and classroom.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that we can and should do more to hasten and strengthen the various placement programmes and initiatives to allow SPED students who complete their school and training to prepare for work in areas where they are keen and able to.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With a lesser student cohort across the entire mainstream education system due to low birth rates in the past decade, I think we should look into having smaller class sizes across our Primary and Secondary Schools.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is without doubt that smaller class sizes do help to enhance and improve the overall learning experience and enhances the student-teacher interaction opportunities for every student.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With the half-life of skills shortening with transformed jobs and new jobs, greater speed to market in terms of skills, competencies, and knowledge is an imperative.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need our Institutes of Higher Learning to transform into Institutes of Continuing Education and Training to work with employers and especially the industry clusters to know the future jobs and the future in-demand skills, so that we can plan, prepare and conduct bite size and modular training in response to market and industry needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I urge MOE to undertake appropriate strategies to help our workers, especially the mature PMEs achieving skills security by supporting them in their pursuit of training opportunities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, Sir, "What would be the ideal education system for Singapore, if we were starting from a clean slate?” This is the question I would like to ask MOE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The world of teaching and learning has been disrupted, like never before.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Thankfully, education technology that the MOE has, such as the Student Learning Space and the Personal Learning Devices (PDL) they had in mind, were already in the works for use by the students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: COVID-19 had significantly compressed the timeline to digitise education; and ground challenges like educator, student and family readiness are not uncommon.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A good mobile app developer, for instance, needs to understand not only programming coding, but also user interface design, content and marketing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The demands of a hybrid job market, for instance, makes cross learnings across departments and disciplines, especially in higher education, not only important but urgent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They dreamt of an end to high stake state exams, physical classrooms and teacher-led mass learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Indeed, if that were the model of future education, then many concerns raised here and outside of this House such as class sizes, excessive tuition, PSLE, Mother Tongue scoring and so on – are issues surrounding the current education model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Past education reviews such as the PERI – the Primary Education Review, the Secondary School Review, ASPIRE, and even Special Education Reviews; were mostly fine tuning of the current system whilst retaining the same structural pillars.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Alas for me, the true train 10 years school system without the PSLE is still a pipe drink for me.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But Chairman, I call upon the wisdom of Harvard Professor Clayton Christensen's renowned work on innovation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The good Prof convinced many senior leaders, some of whom are in our Government, that even the most outstanding companies with established products can become irrelevant unless they know how and when to abandon traditional business practices.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, the need for what he calls, "disruptive innovation".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I totally understand the wisdom of not throwing the "baby out with the bathwater".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, during the COS debates in 2020, MOE announced that Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) would be refreshed, reinforcing the teaching of moral values increasing emphasis on mental health and cyber wellness, engaging students more actively in contemporary issues and being more integrated into subjects and activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is growing recognition that soft skills that are crucial for 21st century employees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am using soft skills here as a convenient broad shorthand for a number of skill-sets such as, firstly, critical thinking and problem solving which top the list of skills many employers believe will grow in prominence in the next five years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And thirdly, resilience and curiosity, which are reported as priced by industry leaders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How can our CCE curriculum help to plug these gaps?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For one, we should cultivate some form of standardised measurement of soft skills, spanning not only tests but project work, classroom interaction and other work streams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After all, we need to build measures of success into our policies so as to ensure that in education, as in all domains, we are striving for outcomes and not just effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I would like to ask how does MOE intend to measure progress towards soft skill formation objectives in the CCE?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would to like to urge greater support for teachers to a progressive reduction in average form class sizes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would better enable teachers to focus on pastoral care for students.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Research has shown that smaller classes may stimulate non-cognitive skills or soft skills, a point I have made in my Parliamentary Adjournment Motion on the subject in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would thus like to suggest that MOE pilot CCE classes and smaller class sizes to study their effects on students' non-cognitive development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Parliamentary colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim will elaborate on the subject of class sizes in his subsequent cut.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Mr Chairman, the Budget Statement described extensive plans for an innovation-driven economy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: To thrive in an innovation-driven economy requires more than the acquisition of technical skills and scientific or professional knowledge, but also a mindset that is ready and able to challenge established norms or widely accepted thinking, not afraid to fail and ever ready to try again, and an eagerness to navigate the unknown.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can the Minister share with us what are the plans to prepare our students for an innovation-driven economy?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Over the years, efforts have been made to move away from a grade-centric education system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: For example, there are no measurable indicators for adaptability, ability to work in teams and across cultures, critical thinking, and so on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Will the Ministry be looking into additional KPIs to measure these desired outcomes?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If so, it would not be a true indicator of engagement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Measuring the engagement rate of grown citizens would be a more accurate indicator.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Here, I declare my interest as an operator of a private school.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: During the course of my work, I came across students who dropped out of Secondary schools but, after working for a few years, decided that they needed to go back to school.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Aiming to enrol in a Polytechnic, they set out to take the "O" Levels in private schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: It is sad to see some give up because they cannot afford it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Homeschooled students also do not get access to core curricular activities (CCAs).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Taiwan's schools embrace homeschooling and schooling kids learning together.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Countries like Israel have a second-chance programme to help students complete their Secondary and diploma education.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As long as our young have the desire to learn, let us give them the necessary support.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Will the Minister allow these students to be attached to mainstream schools for CCAs?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Over the past eight years, my family have gone through three PSLEs, one "O" level and one "A" level.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There will be one more taking "A" level examination this year and the youngest one will be taking hers next year.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Members who are sharp will think that maybe I missed out two "O" levels.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Those who are quicker will know that I did not miss any major milestones in my children's education but because two of them are in the Integrated Programme.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: But I am sure that there may be Members who do not understand what we are talking about because they have no children or their children have long passed their schooling years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Indeed, most of us will only pay attention to or make an effort to understand policies which affect us directly.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, in the area of education, most of us will claim some authority because we ourselves have gone through formal education in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We have our own experience to go by.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The problem is, the personal experience of most parents will be outdated, easily by 20 to 30 years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: For me, I went through the era when PSLE scores are in the 300 to 400s.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I took my Secondary 1 History in Chinese, had to take a compulsory "O" level subject in Religious Knowledge, and could only choose a pure science, pure arts or pure commerce subject combination for my "A" level.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Today, "multiple pathways" have become the lingo and I am a firm believer of that.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: My youngest daughter did not do as well as her two elder siblings in Primary school.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With a 30-point difference in her PSLE score, she could not make it to any of the schools offering the Integrated Programme.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: She went to a school in our neighbourhood, whose cut-off point was some way below her score.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: During her four years there, because she was "within her league", she blossomed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Her confidence and self-esteem improved tremendously and she was offered various exposure and leadership opportunities in school.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I am glad she did really well in her "O" level last year and could make it to any school she wants.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Through a slightly different pathway, she now joins her elder brother, who is doing the last year of his Integrated Programme.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What made us really proud of her is that she did all these years without any tuition.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: She made it with her diligence and discipline and, I would say, by being in a school environment that supported her and one that was suitable for her.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This is not to game the system but to change mindsets so that our young could reap the benefits of the changes and, more importantly, enjoy the learning process and develop positive attitudes that would stay with them for lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A higher AL translates to a poorer PSLE score.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When parents opt for their child to take a Foundation level subject after Primary 4, it will be an uphill climb to get back to Standard level in Primary 6.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Poor grades in school are seldom a full reflection of the student's abilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The quality of instruction they receive and their home environment make a big difference.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some students simply need more encouragement and guidance to do better academically.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What are the objective and subjective criteria that schools use to determine the student's subject level combinations?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How are parents, including those who may be less educated, made fully aware of the impact that taking Foundation level subjects will have on their child's PSLE score?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How do schools ensure that late bloomers will have a fair chance at taking Standard level subjects at the PSLE despite poor examination performance in Primary 4 and Primary 5?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Despite this, residents are still not able to secure a place in a nearby school as the school is oversubscribed in Phase 2C.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I can understand why the Primary 1 Registration Framework needs to accord higher priority to certain groups like siblings as well some priority to other families with ties to the school.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is a maximum number of places that a school can offer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So some tradeoffs will be necessary to enhance open access in all our Primary schools, especially in Phase 2C, for those who live near the school.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, recently, I received feedback on the challenges of securing a place in a school near where students live.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In most cases, it is because the schools nearby are very popular in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In addition, there are many parents who are also former students who would like their children to be part of the school.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister for Education how the Ministry views balancing the priority between alumni and students who live in the neighbourhood, and if there is any on-going review?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Mr Chairman, MOE has been closing schools and reducing its headcount of teachers due to declining birth rates and school enrolments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can the Minister clarify why so many more management staff are needed to manage a declining number of teachers and students?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: What are the targeted number of teachers in the next few years?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: To introduce greater diversity and differentiated learning into our education system, we need smaller class sizes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I mentioned this last October and I feel the need to bring it up again.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: With declining enrolment, it would have been the perfect opportunity to reduce class sizes had we not decreased the number of teachers and NIE intake.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Not only would smaller class sizes provide better outcomes for students, it would be beneficial for teachers as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We ought to care for teachers' emotional and mental loads as well, in addition to their work loads.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Will the Minister consider resuming the recruitment of teachers to previous levels, especially at a time when job opportunities are greatly reduced due to the pandemic?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore currently has one of the highest average class sizes among advanced countries in Primary and Secondary schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the average among industrialised economies is a little more than 20.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in East Asian economies such as Korea and Japan, student numbers in the Primary school classroom only push a little past 25.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, the trend in Singapore has improved over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The pupil-teacher ratio at the Primary level was around 26 at the turn of the millennium compared to 15 today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is hardly satisfactory in light of the fact that these numbers still pale in comparison to countries such as Denmark at 12, Australia at 11 and Luxemburg at nine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While certain banded classrooms are indeed smaller, this does not cover students who are not currently struggling, who arrived there on the basis of supplementary educational support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, some may question, why, in spite of these unflattering resource ratios, our students appear to be able to producing some of the best test scores worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Part of the reason is likely to be our heavy reliance on supplementary education, sometimes pejoratively called the shadow education system, supplied by families directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Private tuition and other supplementary education expenses come up to $112 out of the household's monthly educational expenditures, a little more than 2%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is more than what the average household spends on clothing and air travel and about a quarter of what they spend to be able to put a roof over their heads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is around 10% of the total that the Government spends officially on public education and, to the extent that we believe public education should be largely self-contained, represents an additional and implicit tax on Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, other East Asian societies, including China, Indonesia, Japan and Korea tend to engage more private tutors than other advanced countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Around 70% of students in these aforementioned countries attend after-school lessons in mathematics, for instance – unsurprisingly, I was one of them – compared to less than 20% in countries such as Austria, Canada, Finland and New Zealand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, the disparities between what we devote to public education expenditure is clearly indirectly, if imperfectly, made of four by private supplemental financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even setting our "kiasu" mindset aside, most parents do not have any burning to send their kids onto additional tuition if there are otherwise able to cope with the subjects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Consider how our tuition dollars are predominately spent on subjects where students struggle such as math or languages, and less on humanities such as history or geography.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Smaller class sizes can go a long way toward helping the average Singaporean household reduce their perceived need to engage additional private tuition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, more importantly, smaller class sizes can also help level the playing field.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the evidence in favour of small class sizes for overall student achievement is weak albeit still positive, it is undeniable that individual students can benefit from smaller classrooms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A small number of students release the load on our teachers, thereby freeing them up to pay more attention to students that are falling behind and since lower income households are less likely to be able to allocate additional finances towards tuition just so that their children may stay up to speed, this obviates the need for supplemental private tuition which can prevent students from such households from falling even further behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I am suggesting that the MOE, perhaps, consider capping class sizes at 23 which incidentally is the OECD average and, in particular, for the most tutored subjects such as mathematics as well as languages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is strong feedback from the ground that ranking is not the best way to appraise all job holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are differences in implementation across schools and there is a need for a more standardised system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is also a need for more transparency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the appraisal system should be more formative than punitive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should remove the punitive implications of getting the lower grades.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should create a more nurturing environment for our teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to working with MOE and the unions to improve the performance management system of stacked ranking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: School leaders must give teachers who receive the C- or D grade feedback to improve their performance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, some teachers shared that this feedback only comes after the actual grade has been issued.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some say that little is done to help teachers improve in the course of the school year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar to how students have a mid-year exam to gauge whether they are on the right track, our teachers must also be given feedback prior to receiving their actual grade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are guidelines in place for ROs to give intermittent feedback.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOE currently uses the 360-degree feedback tool more as a developmental tool for leaders to gather feedback rather than as an appraisal tool.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is strong support for implementing a 360-degree feedback to assess the effectiveness of Reporting Officers at all substantive grades.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, as Singapore re-defines our competitive edge by pivoting towards innovation, we will need to create multiple pathways for Singaporeans of all potential to develop and thrive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Achieving this will require the creation of "pathways to excellence" in multiple fields and disciplines, and both public and private tertiary institutions should have roles to play.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore can be proud of a public education eco-system that delivers world-leading education outcomes and boasts some of the world’s best universities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, we are very proud of our public universities eco-system.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But our private education system also has produced high quality providers in specialised areas, such as LASALLE and the Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These specialised institutes are able to deliver excellent outcomes and are seen as leaders in their own field.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Looking globally, we see many examples of private schools offering "pathways to excellence" in high-demand, specialised areas – for example, the Parsons School of Design in New York as well as EHL for hospitality at Lausanne, Switzerland.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Similarly, Singapore can encourage private education institutes to fill talent gaps in the specialised fields and to build best-in-class capabilities in niche areas, and thereby complement the broad-based education offered by our public system.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will enable Singapore’s top quality home-grown PEIs to be independent of their overseas partners and have the autonomy over their curriculum design, development and delivery.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Every year, around 9,000 students graduate from private education institutions offering degree courses in Singapore, while thousands more study in universities overseas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: These are enormous financial commitments for them and their parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In contrast, their peers and local Autonomous Universities spent around $8,200 annually for a non-medical degree after benefiting from tuition grants.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Many Polytechnic graduates feel the pressure to get a degree because better job and salary prospects as they compete in a globalised job market even in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can our AUs continue to open up more places, raising the target cohort participation rate to 50%?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This will allow more deserving Singaporeans who want to attend the AUs to tap on the tuition grant scheme and benefit from the high quality of education offered by our AUs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the concept of meritocracy has been central to Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The implicit assumption in the system assumes that success in life is a deserved outcome to those who have worked hard and upwards, social mobility is possible if you strive and succeed regardless of the socio-economic class that you are born into.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This psyche of attaining success through one's effort and merit has been enshrined much into Singapore's collective consciousness and social fabric and has manifested itself in our perception that attaining a good education is somehow correlated with success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, we should be wary of continuing to chase after GPAs and endorsements of the universities without considering if its training and education is relevant to the job market and, more importantly, to our lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the world we live in today, it is not so much about what you know, as opposed to what you can do and I believe that we just strive to contemporise our university education to reflect this reality.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our university education landscape tends to revolve around a continuous four-year stint of education from 18 to 21 or 22 years of age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Depending on the degree programme, this curriculum tends to be largely theory-based.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some students who have interacted with tell me that they sometimes have difficulty to relating to concepts that were taught in universities because the unable to comprehend how these concepts work in the real world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Students also sometimes take a formulaic approach to concept application, applying their learnings rigidly assuming that the best practices that they have learned in case studies and classes would work in the real world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would help them better appreciate the concept that they have studied in school and allow them to draw practical and operational relevance that are much needed for them to function and blossom in today's university.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, universities could thus be seen as the places of true continuing education where students of different ages and experiences could come and go, taking a continuous short series of short courses and programmes that would enhance what they have already learnt in the real world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I would quote from hon Member Ms Denise Phua's line of "learning anytime, anywhere and at any age".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Along this line, we could also encourage our universities to value educators who bring with them a deep wealth of experience and functional expertise in the corporate world.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Potential to be the best version of him or herself.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In time to come, they will begin life’s salmon run and give it their best shot in their swims upstream.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And yet for a variety of reasons, some of these young ones will stumble along the way.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By any standard, we have done remarkably well in keeping our young ones in school.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the story here on is a little troubling.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And paper qualification that a young person possesses is the marker of his or her intrinsic value, or worse, one that is commensurate with his or her concept of self-worth.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How tragic would that be, if it were true?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have been mentoring ITE students for the past seven years or so, so I have the privilege of interacting with many of them.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deep down in my heart, and I am sure in many of Members' hearts, too, in this Chamber, we all know there is still some truth to this.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is still how many of us frame how we think about education and success.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are students who do well academically, that is, our top 10% in schools, top 10% in everything else in life?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I cannot speak for others, but I do know if I ever were to be assessed for handyman work, I would likely rank amongst the bottom 10%.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And how about an index for street smarts?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hardly think I would go very far in that aspect as well.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps, we should stop labelling youths who are not as academically inclined as the "bottom 10%" or the laggards?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They too have talents; they too have potential that they can show to the world.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Wayne Liu, or DJ Koflow as he is better known, is one stellar example.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When a younger Wayne ran afoul of the law, what the probationer said left a deep impression on him, and I quote, "You don’t have good grades, but you’re a very talented kid.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: You need to find your focus." Today, Wayne is one of our music scene's most established turntablists, well sought after in the region.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I must qualify I am not making a case that one needs to be big in order to be successful.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I recently spoke to Eugene, a teaching assistant and technical officer in a local institution.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Armed with an ITE certificate and his burning passion, he decided to become an audio engineer right after National Service.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a path less travelled, and understandably, family support was lukewarm.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He had met several mentors who took him under their wings and generously guided him along the way.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Eugene's journey in music was heavily driven by passion.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In school, his main motivation to learn was to pick up skills that would help him do well in what he was passionate about, not grades.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Eugene's journey, as well as many others who had taken paths less travelled, is instructive.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we, as a society, change our mindsets about how success is defined and how one gets there?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we, as a society, dump our deep-seated biases and start looking at our youths with a pair of untainted lenses?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we better structure a system that would nurture, mentor and help them uncover and pursue their passions, even in non-mainstream fields?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He said, and I quote, "Human beings are not born once and for all on the day their mothers give birth to them… life obliges them over and over again to give birth to themselves." Mr Chairman, we must enable and empower all our youth, including who are less academically inclined, to be able to reinvent and be the best version of themselves.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, for students from disadvantaged families, Student Care Centres, or SCCs can play a crucial role in ensuring that they get the additional support for their well-being.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to supervision and guidance for their studies, centre staff can help to keep an eye on their health and emotional conditions, and alert the authorities if there are troubling issues affecting these students.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can they be given priority for places at their own schools' SCCs to minimise travelling, particularly for Primary school students?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If their own Primary schools do not have SCCs, if the families wish, can their children be accorded priority for transfers to the nearest schools with SCCs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, can dinners be provided for children from distressed families to minimise food insecurity?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Much credit goes to MOE and all our educators and staff.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Education is the key enabler that imbues values and empowers social mobility.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When we get this right, it is not just the students involved but their families too.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated industry changes and everything needs a rethink and education is no exception.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Second question – the jobs that our students will be doing in the future may not even exist today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The dynamism in the industry expects our graduates to be adaptable, versatile and resilient, as well as having an attitude of being always ready to learn.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, the importance of providing them a broader base education that strengthens their foundation has grown in importance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And my last question is around lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In support of the national imperative to encourage lifelong learning, Polytechnics have built on the existing industry partnerships to develop programmes to support our local Industries and businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What we have found is that SMEs still need help with their skills transformation plans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have one suggestion, which is to second lecturers to selected industries for three to six months or longer, almost like a skills transformer as a service to help SMEs develop the CET training plans for their staff.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The focus on CET for workers is imperative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does MOE intend to further this aspiration?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And in closing, I would like to leave a quote for all the students: "Educators open the door, but you, must enter by yourself."

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Polytechnics and ITEs are a critical part of our education system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not only must the curriculum be dynamic and able to prepare graduates for the future economy, they must also appeal to the diverse learning interests and needs of our students and inspire them to seek out challenging opportunities for them to always learn and grow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As our education system moves to novel approaches like subject-based banding in our schools and dual majors in our Universities, let us not neglect to consider similar approaches for our Polytechnics and ITEs, including the potential to accelerate progression based on performance or dual diplomas.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to ask MOE, as the Member before me, to provide an update on the pathways, progression and curriculum in Polytechnics and ITEs, and how success will be measured.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, may I take the three cuts together?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Thirty years ago, the "typical" route for Normal stream students was to do their "N" levels and get into ITEs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Alternatively, they can do well for "N" levels, get themselves to do the "O" levels next, and then get to the Polytechnics or Junior Colleges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Many of my best students actually come from the ITE route.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Another group that stood out is from the Polytechnic Foundation Programme (PFP).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Many have done well – even better than those that come in from the "O" levels route.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: When I was doing my diploma 25 years ago – yes, 25 years ago – courses were limited to business, IT, or engineering-related one.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Now, we have a variety of courses, from Sports Science all the way to designing games for gamification.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In my previous speeches, I have brought forth the need to review courses in IHLs to cater for the diverse learning needs and interests and better prepare graduates for the future economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister, what are their plans to enhance the current pathways in the IHLs?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: (In Malay):    Language is a reflection of a person’s race, culture and character.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: It also links one’s identity to his or her heritage.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: As Singapore transformed into a developed nation that places importance on using the English language fluently, let us remind ourselves that the major economies in this region do not use English as the lingua franca but our mother tongue languages instead like Malay, Mandarin and Tamil.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Therefore, what policies will the Ministry of Education pursue to preserve the use of mother tongue languages among students so that they will not only appreciate but also understand the importance of mother tongue in their daily lives?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: (In English): One persistent issue that I have been confronted with my students and young residents alike, is mental health – from anxiety to addiction to depression originating from various sources from home, school and the cyberspace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The cyberspace is not just a digital playground.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: It is a source of information or misinformation, and a platform for rich interaction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Our youths use social media pervasively, and they may feel that they must present a particular front to keep up with their friends' fake realities on social media.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: This behaviour may induce unnecessary stress that may affect their mental wellbeing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Additionally, this stress may be compounded and worsened when cyberbullying comes into play.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: It can be as simple as continually muting a fellow classmate in class such that he cannot participate in an online class anymore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Or it can be more serious ones, where they gang up on online social media, target an account, attack them and ridicule these accounts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, as a parent, as an educator, I am naturally concerned.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In my recent speeches, I highlighted the importance of mental and digital literacy to teach our students how to manage their mental wellbeing, protect themselves in cyberspace but most importantly create future generations of social media users who are discerning and uphold an unwritten code of conduct.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Therefore, could the Ministry share their plans to further institutionalise, incorporate, and enhance mental health education and cyber wellness in the current curriculum.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Stresses and confusion brought by physiological and hormonal changes add to the fray, at a time when young people are honing their self-worth and trying to form their own self-identity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When society risks losing young lives to mental health struggles, educators need to understand and nurture our young through their challenges in holistic manners.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps having a trauma-informed care approach to understand the context of students' experiences could be one way.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Educators can benefit from understanding the various ways that trauma appear in children's lives and some of these include poverty, peer victimisation, family violence, racism, homophobia, and lately, what has come to public attention, transphobia.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.02 pm until 3.25 pm.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, youths are highly plugged into issues that surface in Singapore and beyond due to the ease of access to the Internet.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: More often than not, their opinions and knowledge about these issues also tend to come from the Internet.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Constructive guided discussions in school may be an effective way of unpacking these issues.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that the revamped Character and Citizenship Education or CCE curriculum is trying to prepare the students to have these conversations in a sensitive and thoughtful manner.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These topics may include issues, such as bullying, social media use and the navigation of race and religion issues.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this is a good move as students from different backgrounds are able to interact together in the school environment.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, students are generally more comfortable in school, so they tend to be more candid in their responses.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, we are also scared to discuss as may not always be able to deal with what is raised" or "Students indicate that they are comfortable discussing sensitive topics like, for example, race, religion, sexuality but some of the teachers are not.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Then, how do we move forward?" These are just two of the many teachers who have said something similar.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: My own research has shown that they are particularly concerned about the impact of breaking laws, breaching norms, especially important OB markers, and faced with the pressures of national examinations, many do not want to deviate from the prescribed official curriculum.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Controversial issues and incidents can happen at any time and it would be advantageous for all teachers to be able to seize it as a teachable moment when it happens.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This may be an indication of the willingness of teachers in conducting these conversations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic has also made the mental health issue a concern.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People have felt the effects in a number of ways: increased anxiety, worrying about health and a change in lifestyle habits and socialisation because of social distancing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Pressure levels could intensify for people who already face mental health challenges arising from daily stressors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Pastoral counselling is essential in helping students with their mental wellness so that they can deal with their day-to-day mental stress.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sources of this stress can take the form of that which they face in their personal lives due to family and, perhaps, relationships.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, stress can also result from school-related matters, such as juggling multiple commitments – dealing with academic commitments and co-curricular activities and struggling with issues, such as their emerging identity and personality, relationship matters, peer pressure and even bullying.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We tend to assume that it is typically older students, such as those in Secondary school onwards, who are affected by stress and mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it could also be that students in Primary school face their own types of stress, especially in the face of what some see as the "mother of all examinations" – the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be good if schools, even Primary schools, were able to get more trained counsellors and psychologists to cater to the needs of these students facing challenges and difficulties in this area.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Pastoral counsellors do help to manage the mental and emotional wellness of the students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I feel that there is also a need to have career counselling for students as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While career counselling is typically associated with providing students who are graduating from University to help them sort out their professional post-University choices, I feel that it would be good to also provide career counselling to students earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This could be for students who are transitioning from Secondary school to their Junior College and Polytechnic education, as they can then be guided and advised about the choices that they make in the next step of their education journey.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Often, students do not get sufficient guidance in these areas in terms of the industry or the profession in which they are interested.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Professional career counsellors should ideally be industry professionals with the appropriate industry and professional experience – very different from the experience offered by educators or teachers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, these counsellors could also have the industry connections and network to invite industry professionals into the school to help speak to the students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Catering to students' emotional and career needs will help put them on a road to a stable and secure future, giving them hope and a sense of purpose.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that MOE will continue to provide the required support in these areas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mr Chairman, may I take my cuts together?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Home-based learning, more screen time, online lessons, examinations, CCAs, tuition, extra lessons for a myriad of activities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The environment for a student today has become vastly different from the one of the past.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: I am most concerned for the mental well-being of students.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling, too, shared similar concerns as she highlighted the importance of mental well-being and shared how crucial it was for those students who suffer not to feel stigmatised.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Despite COVID-19 and these evolving challenges, MOE has done well to consistently update and roll out new programmes to better prepare our next generation for the challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Recently, there has been an update to the Character and Citizenship Education curriculum.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Back in my time, it was called "好公民".

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Minister Lawrence Wong shared that every teacher is not just a subject teacher but also a teacher of 21st century competencies and a teacher of citizenship and character.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This resonates deeply with me as it is important to ground our students with the values and competencies that will put them in good stead to thrive in an uncertain future, to care for our fellow citizens and community.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The current curriculum of special education is tailored to support children throughout their education roadmap.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As part of any education system, there will be periods of transition between schools and programmes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: These periods of transition may not be easy for many students with special needs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: When not properly managed, they could cause disruption and much time is needed to adapt.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Every child is different and deserves to be given the opportunity to thrive and discover their true potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some may even have special needs and may need more support and guidance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, this should not just translate into giving them special attention and help.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, it is also important to provide opportunities for them to integrate into the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We could start by creating opportunities for them to learn and play alongside typically developing students in school.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am sure many would not disagree with the vision of supporting our children with special needs and creating an inclusive and integrated learning environment for them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, there may be concerns about shortchanging the typically developing children if teachers need to accommodate those with special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand the challenges but I believe there is great value in investing upstream to provide our students with special needs with the skills and preparing them for life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: More importantly, this group presents a potential resource which may not have been fully tapped.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Learning in school should not be just about learning hard skills and knowledge like Mathematics and Science but also about the softer skills and values.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe it is in our interest to nurture a culture of inclusion, respect and understanding, and these values need to be inculcated from an early age.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that much has been done by schools but I believe we can enhance the existing efforts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To this end, I ask that the Ministry look at a few areas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A revised curriculum could then be curated to enhance the student's education experience and better maximise the child's potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Beyond just sending them for training, could we look at understanding the challenges and providing sufficient resources to guide educators in this journey?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should look at how to regularise such interactions and teach students to respect each other and embrace differences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Schools are best placed to create opportunities to normalise acceptance of people with different abilities and celebrate different strengths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I laud all the efforts taken by the Ministry thus far and sincerely hope that the Ministry would continue to build on existing programmes and initiatives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A proportion of these students then move on to Institutions of Higher Learning, or IHLs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on students with SEN at the IHL level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Without proper support, their chances in securing and completing the internships are low.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, seek to find out the success rate of securing and completing internships for students with SEN in IHLs and how MOE is supporting the institutions and these students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, turning to mainstream Primary and Secondary schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Students with SEN in the mainstream schools follow the national curriculum set by MOE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Teachers and supporting Allied Educators often give the feedback that there is insufficient time and expertise to build and coach these students in non-academic life skills, which they often badly need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can MOE update on its plans to provide more support so that students with SEN in mainstream schools are better prepared for their next phase of life – either to the IHLs, the next level of learning, or for work?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Is there another model different from the current model that might work?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many SPED students in SPED schools need a longer pathway or runway to learn both literacy and life skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The runway is even longer with the disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: More than the rest of their peers, SPED school students badly need lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Recent years saw interesting developments in the special education sector: (a) an increasing number of SPED schools in Singapore; (b) an increase in secondment of MOE career mainstream principals to run special schools; and (c) an increase in MOE headquarters' SPED management, control and reporting requirements.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Tight governance, compliance and reporting are all very critical matters whenever resources, public or community, are expended.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But for especially the SPED sector, where challenges abound, the Government needs to find a better way to bring out the best in its disability charity partners and the community assets that the latter can harness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have three suggestions for MOE's favourable consideration: (a) conduct a joint visioning exercise amongst key stakeholder groups on the SPED schools of the future; (b) develop alliances for action to effectively look into how the sector can innovatively better the education and life outcomes for these students; and (c) design and pilot lifelong learning SPED schools with willing partners and sponsors for the major disability groups.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I look forward to MOE's considered and favourable response.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, it is encouraging that inclusion has been a consistent theme in our recent Budgets.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In sports, medals are won in seconds and those fleeting moments belie years of effort.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our training towards inclusion has just begun and I am concerned whether we are committed enough to reach the podium.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Not many of you know that para-athlete Theresa Goh and I represented Singapore in Athens 2004 – I at the Olympics and her in the Paralympics.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I learned about the Paralympic Movement then and, over the years, got to know more para-athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In 2019, I found little hesitance in deciding to become Yip Pin Xiu's coach even though I have never coached anyone with disabilities before.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We share the same passion, spoke the language and I soon learned that we have more similarities between us than differences.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I felt confident in adapting what I know with what she needs to enact her Paralympic success.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Typically, when a child expresses an aspiration to become an Olympian, we can guide the child to pursue this aspiration through CCAs and clubs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Can appropriate advice and encouragement be given to them?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Does the child have to be contented with just inclusive physical education (PE)?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: There is no doubt we need to play the long game for inclusion and I have two suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Most Singaporeans already know what the Olympics are, but not its parallel movement.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, support our educators with additional resources to teach youths.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We should evaluate how we can allocate resources to continue and extend such support to all schools to get us closer to the podium goal of sustainable inclusion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Through some of these programmes, Singaporeans equip themselves with the necessary skills to take up new roles in the in-demand sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry share details on further efforts to support Singaporeans to learn for life through the SkillsFuture movement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As more people stay at home and spend time online, this has led to a surge in interest in online educational content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Being able to attend classes anytime from the comfort of their homes is a boon for many busy adults juggling multiple commitments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will SkillsFuture look into encouraging this trend of learning online, even when safe distancing measures are relaxed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the plans for the next phase of SkillsFuture to facilitate the pursuit of skills mastery and development?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the measures of success for the SkillsFuture initiative?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, we continue to invest in our people and in providing for more support through SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package for our workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of the many upgrading courses available, many are on digital skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These courses need to translate into real changes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we increase the efficacy of these trainings into driving real digital transformation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we consider measuring success through transformation-driven metrics rather than course take-up rates?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A tiered approach can be used, where applicable, to provide basic subsidy for attending the course and enhanced subsidy if the employee drives a change to the business.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The work-from-home trend driven by COVID-19 has accelerated the realisation that work can be done from anywhere in the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: While this is often couched in terms of a warning to workers in terms of higher competition for jobs in our market that could be done from outside Singapore, it is, in fact, also an opportunity, for our workers to take on jobs anywhere in the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: An unfortunate casualty of COVID-19 is that the pace at which we can pursue learning and growth opportunities in the region has decreased, as borders remain closed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Schools have had to cancel overseas learning trips and exchange programmes and some companies have scaled back on their regionalisation and internationalisation ambitions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Chairman, I am grateful for many things in my life but one of the things I am most grateful for is to have had the opportunity to study and work in the US and, for the past few more years, just spend most of my time working with clients in the region.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Besides gaining an understanding of the market and the ability to work on different types of projects, overseas work experience has many other benefits, including learning to work with diverse teams, cultivating an open mind, enhancing independence and adaptability, and gaining a sense of perspective, empathy, humility and gratitude.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: While the benefits are clearly greater when teams are co-located in the market, there is still a lot to be gained from working with virtual teams in another market and I have lived this on my own.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: As a consultant, I used to spend 45 days a year away from home and the circuit breaker seemed like the end of the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But we have adapted and we have learnt that we can still deliver projects and deliver great value – staff teams in any of the countries from regions around the world – with technology.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The Government has recently strengthened the enterprise pillar of the skills eco-system with many exciting reskilling programmes driven by Queen Bee global companies, many of which provide support to place graduates of the programmes into local positions within Singapore firms in their eco-system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: At this point, I should declare that I work for one of such companies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Can we lean in on the Queen Bee global companies that we are partnering with in our various skills programmes to provide opportunities for our students in schools and our trainees in our skills programmes to gain exposure and experience working on projects and internships with teams outside of Singapore, while remaining in Singapore, as the world continues to tackle the COVID-19 pandemic, and perhaps even be considered for employment with companies overseas today, and even more after we are all vaccinated and the opportunities of the world are open for us again?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as CEO of WMI, an education institute.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We witnessed a unique situation, where millions of workers became unemployed on one hand and significant numbers of new jobs created on the other.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The skills mismatch has never been more stark.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst Singapore has managed to keep unemployment at bay with generous job support schemes, many have flagged under-employment as the bigger issue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As Singapore shifts its focus towards recovery and emerging stronger, we need to accelerate support for Singaporeans to pick up skills they need to move into new jobs and new sectors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government, employers and workers need to join forces to embrace reskilling pathways to address the skills mismatch.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: According to a Harvard Business Review article, reskilling refers not only to learning specific job technical skills but also to acquiring core competencies, such as adaptability, communication, collaboration and creativity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The process of reskilling successfully for a new job or to carry out new tasks requires significant commitments of time and investment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, how do we evolve our SkillsFuture training eco-system to adopt similar teaching pedagogy like General Assembly, to provide learners with skills accorded in a more formal learning experience with clear links to job performance outcomes?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With significant job opportunities in the care, digital and green economy, how can we evolve our reskilling pathways to train for skills needed in these sectors?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The set-up of the industry academies to provide high quality certified courses to support acquisition of skills and capabilities in demand by industry is critical to support reskilling efforts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The introduction of SkillsFuture Queen Bee companies is a good initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, much has been said about the wide-reaching impact of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has forced us to question assumptions we have long taken for granted and it has changed the way we live, work, study and play.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In many countries, the impact has been felt sharply by students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Schools have been closed for months; some students have not seen their teachers face-to-face for more than a year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Worse, the issue has been politicised in some places, creating sharp divisions between parents, teachers and even teacher unions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For this, we owe a debt of gratitude to all our educators for their hard work and sacrifices, their ability to adapt and respond quickly, and their dedication to keep our schools and students safe.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I would like to put on record in this House my thanks to all our educators in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond the immediate impact it has had on our schools, COVID-19 has added greater urgency to our "Learn for Life" movement and crystallised what our priorities are moving forward.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Ms Denise Phua said, it has given us an opportunity to re-imagine what our education system could be like in a post-COVID-19 world, and I assure her that that is something we are committed to doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are not constrained by legacy thinking or existing ways of doing things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: No programme or structure in our education system is beyond scrutiny or re-examination.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We may put back the stone after turning it over and there may well be good reasons for the stone to be there, but we will continue to pick it up again and again and we will take a closer look from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, since joining MOE, the question I have been asked the most is: what can I do to better prepare for a more uncertain, turbulent and volatile future?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I think many young people and their parents hope for some guidance on what course of study would give them a head-start.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, in fact, there is no "right" or "ideal" subject to choose.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Whatever a student studies in school, the content knowledge will need to be constantly refreshed and updated throughout their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, many young people today want to learn how to code and that is a good thing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A few years later, they will have to confront new apps, devices and programming languages.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, students have to be prepared to constantly upgrade themselves and take on multiple jobs throughout their lifetimes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, some of the jobs they will do in the future may not even exist today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In such a world, what is more important is the ability to learn how to learn, to keep on learning and re-learning and to enjoy doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want our students to read widely, ask critical questions, analyse data, formulate ideas and to communicate well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Mr Patrick Tay said just now, we want our system to be ready, relevant and resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we continue to improve, to learn from other systems and to try out new approaches.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Whatever changes we make, we do so carefully and thoughtfully, not just blindly copying others, but making sure there are genuine benefits and value.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is something several Members spoke about earlier, including Ms Denise Phua, Mr Leon Perera and Ms Hazel Poa, and I agree with them that it is important to develop these skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The competencies that matter for success in the real world go well beyond academic abilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not so easy to test or develop KPIs for such skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The outcomes are not always easily measured, and must be observed over time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In schools, our teachers actively look out for these traits in our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And what is encouraging is that our students do outperform their peers in some areas, like cross-cultural skills and dispositions, and collaborative problem solving.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of course, there is also room to improve in other areas, like adapting to new challenges and the preparedness to embrace failure.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we have made progress but there are some areas where we can do better and we will continue to do more to emphasise 21CCs throughout the entire education journey.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The revised curriculum will further anchor our students on strong values, teach them to appreciate diverse perspectives, strengthen their mental resilience and make them more cyber-savvy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: CCE will not just be delivered through dedicated lessons.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it will also be interwoven more deliberately throughout school lessons and activities, as part of the everyday school experience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And Minister of State Sun Xueling will provide more details later in her speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also learning from our experience with Home-Based Learning, or HBL, and are incorporating Blended Learning strategies in schools – where students learn not just in classrooms, but also at their own pace at home, enabled by technology.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is between 10% to 20% of curriculum time, depending on the level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The key motivation for doing this is to give our students more flexibility to chart their own learning and to equip them with important skills, like initiative, discipline and self-management.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides curriculum coverage, HBL days will also include dedicated time for student-initiated learning, where students can explore areas of personal interest outside the curriculum, like learning a foreign language or musical instrument.
